rationale:
Evidence: iteration 6 is the best raced design (570.4). Moving the five sensors forward from y=0.03 to y=0.05 m raised the oval finish rate from 10/20 to 20/20, the s-bend finish rate from 0/20 to 9/20, and slalom progress from 0.28 to 0.41. Sensor lead distance is the lever that has worked. Slalom is still 0/20, ending off track with max_error near the 0.06 m limit and steering_oscillation about 0.30. Mean rms_error is only about 0.02, so the robot tracks well on average and fails at sudden alternating bends, which points to late correction at turn-in.

Change (one variable): sensor y moves from 0.05 to 0.07 m, the upper end of the allowed range. This extends the look-ahead so the correction starts earlier at the slalom bends. Everything else is held at the iteration 6 values: x spacing -0.04 to 0.04 with 16 mm footprints, kp 3.0, kd 0.8, ki 0.02, base_speed 1.3, mass 0.6 kg, last_direction line loss. This isolates the look-ahead effect against the best baseline. Iteration 7 had this same plan but never raced, so it is still untested.

Expected result: slalom and s-bend max_error falls, slalom progress rises above 0.5, and s-bend finishes improve. Oval should stay near 100% completion.

Hypotheses: (a) if slalom still exits at max_error about 0.06 with no gain from y, steering authority is the limit, so kp should rise to about 3.3 with kd held. (b) If steering_oscillation rises above 0.35, the far-forward sensors are amplifying jitter, so kd should drop toward 0.6. (c) If the oval stops completing, the forward lead is overshooting on straights, so y should return to about 0.06.

Measurements wanted: all per-track metrics, so the look-ahead effect can be read separately for oval, s-bend and slalom.
